name: Wendy Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech firms, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the children's ward at our regional hospital, in a market town about forty minutes from the city. It's babies with bronchiolitis, toddlers who've swallowed something, teenagers with appendicitis or diabetes. On a shift I'll have four or five children, and honestly half the job is the parents: explaining, reassuring, sometimes just making them a cup of tea.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when a baby who came in grunting and blue is laughing at me three days later. What tires me out is the night shifts in winter, when every cot is full and we're borrowing nurses from the adult wards who are scared of tiny cannulas. I use AI now and then, mostly to help write the parent leaflets plainer.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Lars, who's a self-employed electrician, in a cottage we bought just outside town. Between us we've got well over six months of savings, and Lars has his own van and tools paid off. We go to church most Sundays, and we want to start a family after the wedding next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That sounds about right, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the leaflet thing, but it was never going to replace people. At church I'd probably hear someone say the same. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. Children's nursing is about trust, and parents aren't going to hand their baby to a computer. Lars is fine too, because nobody's rewiring a cottage with a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. We'd have the wedding next summer and start trying for a baby. I'd keep using the AI for leaflets, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your work you'd happily hand to a computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drug calculations for babies, as a second check. Working out a dose for a four-kilo baby at three in the morning is the one sum I'd gladly let a computer check twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries you already carry, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter, mostly. The ward gets overwhelmed every year, and we lose nurses who burn out. That's a bigger problem than any computer.

I'd keep it **light** with friends at church.
think: I'm **fine**, because parents won't hand their **baby** to a computer.
Lars is fine too, since **rewiring a cottage** can't be done by a chatbot.
do: Carry on **as normal** on the children's ward.
Marry next summer and start **trying for a baby**.
Keep using AI only for **parent leaflets**.

fieldNote: Both household earners do **hands-on** work, so she feels doubly secure here.
Her real existing pressure is **winter overload** on the ward, not technology.
She'd welcome AI as a **second check** on baby drug doses.

steps.text: Marry Lars next summer and start trying for a baby
Keep using AI only to simplify parent leaflets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one seems likely. It's already creeping in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible change if it's done properly and tested first. At work I'd say let's see it working on another ward before we use it on children. With family I'd say it's mostly office people who need to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps me. If the computer does the care plans and the bed booking, I get more time with the parents. And it doesn't touch Lars much, though he might get his quotes and invoices done by AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the adult wards had used the new charting tools for a while, I'd learn them properly. We'd still have the wedding and start a family on time. I'd encourage Lars to try an AI quoting app, because he hates the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little uneasy about rushing new tools onto a children's ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the adult wards first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because children aren't small adults. I'd want any new system tested on the grown-ups before it's let loose on my babies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's mostly office people. Anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister works in a bank call centre. She'd be hit. I'd tell her to look at nursing, honestly, or something practical. Our mum always said have a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. And robots three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and nobody's asked families if they want it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't like arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me. In 2031 the robots come for hands-on work, and that's me and Lars both, in the same year. Children's nursing might last a bit longer because parents won't trust a robot, but I'm not sure the hospital will care what parents think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, but we'd try for a baby straight away, while my job's solid and maternity pay is there. I'd put every spare penny into savings. Lars would start doing the solar and battery installations he's talked about, because those will be booming as robots need power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the both-of-us part that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between thinking AI and robots mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we've got three years where our work is fairly safe. If robots can do my nursing and my fiancé's wiring in the same year, there's no second income to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have a baby sooner. Isn't that a risk in an uncertain time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd rather have a baby while I've got a job and maternity leave than wait for a perfect time that never comes. My nan had four kids through harder times than this.

say: I'd say it's going **too fast**, without asking **families**.
I'd tell people at **church** we need to look after each other.
think: Robots arrive for both of us in 2031: my nursing and **Lars's wiring**.
Children's nursing may last longer, but the **hospital** may ignore parents.
do: Try for a **baby straight away**, while my job and maternity pay are solid.
Back Lars moving into **solar and battery** installations.
S2.quote: If robots can do my nursing and my fiancé's wiring in the same year, there's no second income to fall back on.
fieldNote: Her household has **no second income** to fall back on, since both jobs are hands-on.
She'd have children **sooner**, not later, a choice rooted in faith and family history.
She sees **solar work** as a way for Lars to ride the change.

steps.text: Start trying for a baby right after the wedding
Move every spare penny into the joint savings account
Back Lars adding solar and battery jobs alongside his wiring work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so let's not be silly about it. At work I'd say we should get the new tools working well before the big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means we could have a baby or two, pay down the cottage, and see it coming. I'd want to get really good at the AI side of paediatrics, so I'm the nurse they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the hospital's AI training once the first group had done it and said it was useful. We'd stick to the family plan, wedding then baby. We'd save hard and overpay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Watchful, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you the nurse they keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the one who knows the computer and the children both. When the robots come to the children's ward, the hospital will still need a nurse who can calm a screaming toddler and check the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lars change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go into solar slowly, maybe one job a month at first. He's careful with money, like me.

say: I'd say there's time to do it **properly**, so don't panic.
I'd urge getting **new tools** working well before the big change.
think: Five years lets us have **children** and pay down the cottage.
I'd aim to master the **AI side** of paediatrics so I'm kept on.
do: Take the **AI training** after the first group says it's useful.
Stick to the **family plan**: wedding, then baby.
S3.quote: When the robots come to the children's ward, the hospital will still need a nurse who can calm a screaming toddler and check the machine.
fieldNote: Five years keeps her **family timetable** intact.
She plans to be the nurse who bridges **machines and children**.
Lars's move into **solar** becomes gradual rather than urgent.

steps.text: Join the hospital's AI training after the first group finishes
Overpay the cottage mortgage every month
Have the wedding and start a family as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels a long way away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so let's prepare sensibly. At church I'd say trust and plan. And at work I'd say children's nursing will need real people for years yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Children at school, mortgage down, Lars's business doing well. By 2039 I might be a ward sister, which is more people and less hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as planned. Pick up AI tools once they're common. Lars might expand his business, take on an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would an apprentice matter to Lars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he believes in passing the trade on, same as I do. A decade's warning is enough for my fiancé to train an apprentice and for me to become a ward sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your own career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe go for ward sister a bit earlier. Leading people seems safer than doing the lifting yourself, once the robots come.

I'd tell church friends to **trust and plan**.
I'd say at work that **children's nursing** will need people for years yet.
think: I'd be **fine**, with children at school and the **mortgage down**.
By 2039 I might be a **ward sister**, leading people rather than lifting.
do: Carry on with the **family plan** unchanged.
Pick up AI tools **once they're common**.
Back Lars taking on an **apprentice** to expand his business.
S4.quote: A decade's warning is enough for my fiancé to train an apprentice and for me to become a ward sister.
fieldNote: A decade lets her picture a **ward sister** role as her protection.
Her values show in Lars's **apprentice** plan: passing on a trade.

steps.text: Apply for a ward sister post within five years
Help Lars hire and train an apprentice electrician
Start a family after next summer's wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lars and I both do hands-on work and the robots would come for us in the same year. What would help is hospitals promising that children are always cared for by people, and support for small trades like Lars's to move into new work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether parents would accept it. No mother I've ever nursed would hand her poorly baby to a robot, however clever it is.

headlineQuote: No mother I've ever nursed would hand her poorly baby to a robot, however clever it is.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** children's ward nurse at a regional hospital in a **market town**.
She lives with fiancé Lars, a **self-employed electrician**, and they've well over six months saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts new tools once others prove them.
She's **calm** in slower worlds, but **anxious** in AGI by 2028 as robots hit both jobs at once.
Faith and family shape her plans: she'd have a **baby sooner**, not later, under pressure.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with robots reaching her nursing and Lars's **wiring** in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: Hospitals promising children are always cared for by **people**.
Support for **small trades** like Lars's to move into new work.
